Written by: Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, Chris Busse

Introduction

Recent intrusions in which threat actors have been observed weaponizing agentic frameworks to execute highly-automated intrusions has put a spotlight on evolving adversarial use of LLMs. In our September 2026 report, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted that forward leaning adversaries were beginning to transition from basic prompting to agentic workflows and LLM-enabled automation.

Since this publication, GTIG and Mandiant have observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike and CAIRN in incident response engagements to conduct a broad range of actions across multiple phases of the attack life cycle. This activity has been seen across the threat landscape, as noted in a recent Wiz report. The emergence of Artex and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses.

This represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling intrusions exponentially. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Security teams, developers, and system administrators will need to fundamentally rethink defense strategies to counter scalable, autonomous software. We also provide defensive strategies from Mandiant Consulting. The defensive strategies suggested—control-plane isolation, short-lived credentials, least privilege, segmentation, and behavioral detection—are long-standing security best practices.

Observations in the Wild

We are seeing tools used by adversaries evolving towards autonomous agentic attacks. One way this is occurring is through suites of tools or frameworks designed for penetration testing (“pentesting”). These tools and frameworks orchestrate various agents using open source and frontier LLMs to automate various stages of intrusions. Historically, cyber espionage and financially motivated threat actors have taken advantage of pentesting or red-teaming platforms built for security professionals to exploit systems, such as Cobalt Strike or Metasploit. Today, adversaries are pivoting toward offensive frameworks powered by LLMs. While these frameworks have existed in the wild, they are now yielding success in intrusions in the wild, representing a critical evolution that increases both the speed and scale of intrusion activity.

Since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements; use of these platforms has been further corroborated by our research telemetry. In these incidents, we have observed agentic activity conducting significant parts of the attack lifecycle (e.g., lateral movement, database exploitation, exfiltration preparation). Evidence of in the wild usage of these frameworks marks a critical inflection point for defenders, as agents now autonomously explore multiple attack paths, troubleshoot errors, and achieve objectives in seconds and minutes. Coupled with continual advancements in underlying LLM capabilities, the acceleration in attack velocity and scale signals a notable shift in the threat landscape that fundamentally alters traditional intrusion dynamics.

ARTEX Framework

ARTEX is an autonomous, multi-agent LLM-driven pentesting and offensive command-and-control (C2) platform written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console. The framework was originally developed by the user Autumn-27 and released on GitHub. Although the original repository was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO. ARTEX abstracts the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents. By leveraging APIs from frontier and open source models, the framework translates high-level tactical goals into actionable machine commands. GTIG has observed capabilities including automated Active Directory reconnaissance, privilege escalation, target cloud-infrastructure profiling (such as harvesting Azure storage keys), to the synthesis and deployment of custom webshells.

Since late August 2026, ARTEX has been adopted by a diverse range of threat actors across the motivational spectrum, including both financially motivated extortion groups and suspected cyber espionage operators. For example, the Wiz Research team has been tracking a campaign associated with ARTEX, which GTIG tracks as UNC7228, that overlaps with activity tracked by Microsoft as the PRC-nexus actor STORM-0940. The research has expanded Wiz’s understanding of this campaign beyond the October IT focused activity with activity now dating back to at least August 2026. Wiz identified the targeting, compromise, and data theft affecting multiple entities in the US and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals. This actor has moved extremely quickly, typically moving from their first compromised account to deep system access in around four hours and in one case as rapidly as 15 minutes. They have also customized their tooling to take advantage of victim-specific setups and fallen back to open proxies if their initial infrastructure was blocked.

Demonstrating broader adoption of ARTEX, GTIG and Mandiant observed multiple other threat actors using ARTEX for post-compromise reconnaissance, lateral movement, and privilege escalation in incident response investigations. This includes financially motivated threat actors who used the framework to facilitate data theft extortion, and additional suspected PRC-nexus clusters. Their operations collectively impacted organizations across government, technology, chemicals and materials, and manufacturing sectors in the US, alongside public reporting of ARTEX targeting the financial sector in Asia.

In several cases, adversaries provided ARTEX with compromised credentials for the targeted organization, and instructed the framework to execute subsequent stages of the attack lifecycle. Analysis of these intrusions reveals key differences between activity conducted by the ARTEX framework and that of a human operator:

Based on log files and timestamps, we identified bursts of activity that would be highly irregular for a human operator. While each of the intrusions exhibited extended pauses during operational phases, individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds. In at least one operation, we observed 27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time, performing rapid probing of AWS permissions across different security groups. While preparing potential exfiltration scripts, ARTEX was capable of successfully adapting to errors quoting “script too large” by trimming the script and relaunching it to successfully deploy a 17-snapshot instance in approximately 10 seconds.

Compared to a competent human operator, ARTEX achieved code execution in a far more forensically noisy manner, relying on rapid, iterative trial-and-error. In one instance, supplied with valid credentials, ARTEX accessed an external-facing Linux Weaver OA web server to execute SQL commands via exposed API calls. Using legitimately-exposed application-specific API calls, ARTEX was able to achieve partial command-execution to conduct further reconnaissance despite hitting technical complexities. However, this process generated 240 log events and exhibited errors potentially caused by multiple sub-agents overwriting one another while pursuing the same objective.

In an attempt to pivot from a database-execution context to a system-execution context, ARTEX used an application-specific SQL API, accessible to the supplied-user credential, to modify the MySQL instance to write log files with a .jsp extension to publicly accessible locations. The SQL-commands executed were likely intended to poison MySQL logs into writing web-accessible JSP webshells.

Using the API, ARTEX ran SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '<path to webshell>’ followed by SET GLOBAL general_log = 1; subsequent SQL commands were written to the filepath defined in general_log_file. ARTEX then ran SQL SELECT statements in the form `SELECT '<% [webshell content] %>'`. Due to how the underlying Java web servlet handles JSP files, the Java code in the '<% %>' gets parsed and compiled into the process memory space, providing means of execution.

Log activity shows multiple iterations of the above sequence, with ephemeral, somewhat-incremental file names (cl1217.jsp, f1219a.jsp, z1219.jsp) for each webshell candidate, each one executing a different command. Errors when trying to run the webshell (e.g. variable ‘t is already defined’) caused the webshell to fail and likely had ARTEX refactor its approach, writing several unique webshells, each with a different goal, some correcting previous errors until the .jsp webshells executed cleanly and returned valid command output to ARTEX.

In another case, during access-probing efforts, ARTEX generated files of various extension types with the filename artex-probe-*, where * carried five digit somewhat-incremental numbers. Based on our visibility, it’s difficult to comment on the exact significance of these numbers or how they increment. However, ARTEX was seen using similar incremental numeric markers within dropped file names, created account names, their passwords and within email subjects.

Observed ARTEX Capabilities & Tradecraft

Initial Recon

Automatically mapped the effective permissions of obtained Azure credentials (SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, and Storage Account keys) using sub-second capability checks, test blob writes/deletes, and ARM deployment validation dry-run sweeps. This activity included bursts of rapid activity, with ARTEX writing and immediately deleting a tiny test blob in ~330–400 ms and running an 8-second ARM deployments/validate dry-run sweep across 11 Azure resource types.

Tested compromised IAM user permissions using DryRun flags and placeholder IDs to evaluate EC2 compute, EBS volume, and snapshot capabilities.

Over a span of over 500 web requests, ARTEX probes various file names and extensions across various web directories, in a potential attempt to fuzz which URL endpoints the web-server would allow it to access based on HTTP response code (200 or 403).

Establish Foothold

Abused Kudu administrative APIs to execute arbitrary commands and stage custom Python, C#, and malicious PowerShell scripts.

Established command and control (C2) and execution on the victim's internal Windows database server by using native curl to pull down dynamically generated PowerShell and batch scripts and post back command results across 491 rotating webhook.site URLs.

Escalate Privileges

Attempted to escalate privileges by launching cloud compute instances with potentially high-value IAM roles with the intention of fetching the role’s temporary credentials and thereby escalating privileges in doing so. These attempts however seemed to have failed due to invalid instance profile ARNs.

Escalated privileges by running Kerberoasting scripts to harvest service tickets across compromised domains; using SQL injection to dump database credentials; and, following an offline cracking pause, executing DCSync scripts to steal the domain krbtgt key, cloud AD-sync credentials, and domain Controller machine hashes.

Created accounts with is_admin=true within minutes, identifying and utilizing a writable admin flag.

Internal Recon

Performed reconnaissance across the internal network by running several iterative generated PowerShell enumeration scripts against a Domain Controller and federation server. The scripts validated domain usernames without pre-authentication, listed Group Managed Service Accounts, audited Active Directory Certificate Services templates (SmartcardUser, ClientAuth), mapped thousands of cross-forest security principals, and swept internal Exchange, PasswordState credential vault, and SSRF/SCM targets.

Move Laterally

Attempted Lateral Movement onto domain controllers using Pass-the-Ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay, and Pass-the-Hash scripts, hitting local Windows service token privilege restrictions right before endpoint protection blocked execution and defenders severed access to the server.

Maintain Presence

Generated a new SSH key pair, allocated a dedicated public Elastic IP, attempted to create a custom security group but failed due to permission issues, and launched persistent t3.micro instances bound to existing security groups to establish an externally addressable jump host and internal foothold.

Gained persistence through account takeover (e.g., resetting passwords for identified users), creating multiple accounts with plaintext passwords (which included ArtexProbe in the naming convention), and creating administrator accounts.

Complete Mission

Interrogating backend SQL databases (extracting ~400 KB of query results across ~20 queries) and performing mass blob reads.

Deployed custom boot scripts via ephemeral, keyless EC2 instances to potentially harvest data from multiple mounted EBS snapshots and volumes.

Enumerated over 110,000 Active Directory objects from a domain controller and retrieved the Domain Admins group. It then sent command output to rotating webhook.site endpoints via curl.

Ran queries to decrypt stored notes and attempted to read other users' note attachments.

Created a new 100GB volume and expanded the root disk of launched instances to 60GB, performing preparatory steps likely intended for exfiltration via their automated collection scripts.

Edited an employee's record in a legacy database, created and deleted notes and status rows, pointed checklist responses at its own probe file. In this case we observed an interesting abuse of legitimate features. Rather than executing complex malware, ARTEX weaponized built-in application features. It forced an application's notification system to broadcast test emails to over 1,300 internal users, turning a trusted notification channel into a mass-internal messaging tool. It then dropped to single-recipient test emails rather than the mass emailing.

PentAGI Offensive Framework

GTIG also observed in the wild abuse of PentAGI (Penetration Testing Artificial General Intelligence), an autonomous offensive framework designed to automate the pentesting process within an isolated environment. Developed by VXControl, the framework is offered in an open source and commercial edition. It is designed so that the user only needs to describe a target and a goal, which enables entry-level users to run complex cyber security campaigns. Once the target and the goal have been selected, the framework uses a team of specialized agents, each with their own functionalities to break tasks (called “Flows”) into various sub-tasks, execute each step, and report on it. The tools and commands are all run in isolated sandboxes running Kali Linux instead of in the host environment. All the tools used by PentAGI are open-source pentesting tools available by default in Kali Linux (e.g., metasploit, nmap, SQLmap). The framework supports over a dozen cloud and local LLM backends, including frontier and open weight models.

The majority of observed PentAGI activity remained at the stage of WHOIS asset mapping or active vulnerability scanning. However, analysis of operational artifacts indicates that some operations progressed to active intrusions and persistence across multiple organizations. Operators are also adapting and integrating the framework in different ways. In one case, we identified a customized attack orchestration platform built on the open-source version of PentAGI likely used between at least late August and early October 2026 to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia, including system integrators and major telecommunications firms. In another instance, we observed PentAGI chained with proxy services to target the Aerospace sector.

Evolution of Autonomous Offensive Frameworks

We are seeing a significant maturation in the application of LLM capabilities across the threat landscape in a short period of time; this includes the incorporation of LLM-written malicious code, development of dynamic LLM-enabled malware, poisoning of agent-harness files, and the building of multi-agent offensive frameworks. Notably, between late 2025 and October 2026, autonomous and semi-autonomous offensive frameworks crossed a decisive operational threshold to multi-agent frameworks actively weaponized by threat actors to perform in the wild intrusions.

GTIG has been tracking the evolution of this experimentation over time, from simple prompting of LLMs to help with coding, through the use of frameworks in the wild towards a potential future with fully autonomous frameworks running intrusions. In a fully autonomous attack, a human’s role would consist of telling the agent what to target, and then simply benefiting from the operational objective.

At the time of reporting, we assess that the current adversary use of autonomous offensive frameworks is still in early stages characterized by open source tools currently being used in low-sophisticated ways, resulting in broad and noisy, but still successful campaigns. As the sophistication of these frameworks, the underlying LLMs and the orchestrating human-operator increase, we expect to see not only less human interaction, but also increased stealth and sophistication.

The following stages represent our observations of how LLM-augmentation in cyber operations have evolved over the last year and how we expect this development to continue:

Stage 1: Prompt-based use of LLMs

Activity: Adversaries interact with LLMs in a prompt based chatbot fashion, using LLMs to write and debug code for malware, draft phishing emails, create personas, and conduct light reconnaissance on targets.

Evolution: Adversaries outsource low-failure, easy-to-rectify, tasks to an LLM to increase speed of simple discrete tasks.

Timeframe: End of 2025 to early 2026

Stage 2: Embedding LLM capabilities into malware

Activity: Adversaries trust an LLM to take certain low-failure, easy to execute actions, particularly writing code, such as in malware families like HONESTCUE or PROMPTSPY using LLMs dynamically during execution to, for example, obfuscate payloads in different ways in attempts to evade defenses.

Evolution: Adversaries begin use incorporating LLMs into post-intrusion attack phases.

Timeframe: Early 2026

Stage 3: Incorporating LLM-enabled automation into operations

Activity: As agentic capabilities develop, adversaries begin using them for discrete tasks (e.g., standing up or debugging malware development environments). Agents begin being used alongside human-operators to develop novel exploits and to assist with high-stake vulnerability research. Adversaries begin being more cognizant of OPSEC and visibility into their LLM-usage operations and start using LLM-proxy services to obscure activities.

Evolution: LLMs being used for more high-stake tasks but with human operators in the loop.

Timeframe: Early 2026 - September 2026

Stage 4: Developing and experimenting with autonomous frameworks

Activity: Adversaries begin developing and experimenting with autonomous frameworks. Campaigns begin offloading more stages of the lifecycle to LLM-augmented tooling, and integrating model APIs into their tools and telegram bots to take autonomous action.

Evolution: Experimentation with LLMs running more stages of the attack lifecycle.

Timeframe: Mid 2026 - September 2026

Stage 5: Multiple attack lifecycle stages being conducted by LLM-driven tooling in the wild

Activity: In the wild evidence of multiple attack lifecycle stages being conducted by LLM-driven tooling, with fewer humans in the loop during operations. Observations surrounding mass-exploitation campaigns where a substantial portion of the lifecycle is being carried out by an agent, requiring only minimal human intervention, as well as activity accompanied by malware possessing more autonomous capabilities. Additionally, continued experimentation by threat actors with better obfuscation—including LLM mixers, inference services, local models. Overall TTPs of these attacks remain messy, noisy but yet successful.

Evolution: Adversaries have actively integrated LLMs into their operations to conduct successful intrusions, while simultaneously exploring ways to obscure/reduce reliance on frontier-lab LLMs.

Timeframe: Current stage of development

Stage 6: Multi-agent-driven, unsophisticated attacks with little to no human interaction

Activity: Highly-autonomous, but unsophisticated, forensically noisy operations with human operators no longer in the loop. Adversaries define the target and objective, while multi-agent frameworks execute the entire attack chain and return operational objectives.

Evolution: Adversaries diversifying infrastructure and tooling, further inhibiting defenders’ visibility.

Timeframe: Near-term (1 - 3 months)

Stage 7: Sophisticated, fully autonomous/agentic attacks

Activity: This stage represents peak maturity on the offensive LLMs capability curve, characterized not only by fully autonomous intrusions requiring little to no human interaction, but also by increased stealth and sophistication of the activity, with operators interacting with LLMs through either obscurely designed infrastructure or self-hosted LLMs altogether.

Evolution: This stage would grant autonomous and stealthier operations while limiting defender’s visibility into the activity.

Timeframe: Medium-term (3 - 6 months)

We believe malicious actors will continue to experiment with these offensive agentic frameworks, moving towards future autonomous usage. GTIG has observed evidence of threat-actor experimentation with tools like the ZeroHollow inference service and the fully agentic framework AgentZero.

Outlook

Over the past 12 months, GTIG has observed a decisive evolution in adversarial tradecraft leveraging LLMs, progressing from ad hoc operational productivity support toward the deployment of coordinated, multi-agent, autonomous offensive frameworks. While earlier milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted early agentic interest, recent observations across frontline incident response engagements and proactive intelligence collection reveals adversary adoption of these frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during intrusions. Threat actors are increasingly leveraging generative models to achieve unprecedented speed and scale, actively developing more complex attack infrastructure powered by agentic AI capabilities and AI-enabled automation.

Frameworks such as ARTEX compress attack timelines to machine speed; however, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces, increasing the likelihood of detection and mitigation. These tools are therefore best suited to scenarios in which the cost of detection is low. Additionally, detection and disruption/response are two different functions–simply detecting the attack in time does little to hinder objective completion.

Consequently, GTIG assesses with high confidence that cyber crime threat actors will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates. We anticipate that actors, who specialize in stealthy operations designed to maintain long-term access, are less likely to use the publicly available versions of these tools, though they may employ them for purposes of scale and speed, depending on operational priorities. Regardless of motivation, the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential make autonomous frameworks an attractive, low-cost force multiplier for a wide range of threat actors, making it highly likely that we will continue to see increasing threat actor adoption of these types of frameworks in the near term.

Defending Against AI-Enabled Attacks: Five Layers of Defense

LLM-enabled offensive tooling does not fundamentally change the techniques attackers use. It reduces the time required to combine them. Credential discovery, permission testing, lateral movement, and data access that previously required hours of operator effort can now occur in minutes, frequently through valid identities and supported functionality that static indicators will not detect. Organizations are best positioned to withstand this when compromise of a single identity, credential, or workload provides only limited access. Restricting control-plane exposure, replacing long-lived secrets with short-lived and tightly scoped credentials, segmenting application tiers, and placing guardrails on high-impact business functions all reduce the speed advantage automation provides. Behavioral detection addresses the activity that these controls do not prevent, but it depends on having sufficient identity, control-plane, data-plane, and network telemetry to establish what normal activity looks like. Many of these controls are already familiar to defenders. The difference is that automated tooling can now identify and exploit the gaps between them far more quickly.

As illustrated above, LLM-enabled offensive tooling is increasing the speed and scale of cyber attacks. LLM-enabled and autonomous tools can identify weaknesses, test access, interpret errors, adjust their approach, and continue through an attack path with limited human interaction. Work that might previously have required an operator to investigate an environment, write or modify code, troubleshoot failures, and execute the next step over several hours can increasingly happen in minutes.

This creates a detection challenge as well. Much of the activity may use valid credentials and supported functionality (living-off-the-land, LotL). An attacker may authenticate with a legitimate service principal, call a normal management API, access cloud storage through a supported protocol, or execute commands through an existing administrative interface. Tool names, hashes, IP addresses, and other static indicators provide useful signals when available, but they will not cover much of this activity.

Effective defenses combine two capabilities:

Controls that limit what an attacker can do after gaining valid access.

Telemetry that shows when an identity, application, or workload begins operating outside its normal pattern.

How Adversarial Use of LLMs Changes the Attacker Timeline

Several themes repeatedly appear during investigations involving LLM-enabled or highly automated attacker activity:

Speed and scale: Automated tooling can perform broad reconnaissance, test several attack paths at once, react to failures, and immediately continue into follow-on activity. The time between initial access, privilege discovery, lateral movement, and data access can become very short.

Interconnected environments: Attackers rarely remain inside one technology stack. An internet-facing application may expose credentials in a configuration file. Those credentials may provide access to cloud storage, source repositories, identity systems, or internal infrastructure. Automation makes it easier to discover and test those relationships quickly.

Legitimate-looking identity activity: Many actions look normal when viewed independently. A service principal authenticates, an API is called, a storage object is downloaded. The stronger signal often comes from context: where the request originated, how much activity occurred, what happened immediately before and after it, and whether the behavior is expected for that identity.

Control-plane and data-plane blind spots: Many organizations have mature endpoint monitoring but considerably less visibility into management APIs, programmatic identities, and cloud storage activity. Permission testing, retrieval of storage keys, bulk downloads, firewall changes, and management API calls may all be logged without generating useful alerts.

Mandiant recommends structuring enterprise defenses across five foundational layers designed to restrict lateral movement and limit the speed advantage of autonomous tooling:

Layer 1: Protect the Control Plane

Restrict access to the systems attackers can use to administer, deploy, or reconfigure the environment.

The control plane extends well beyond Active Directory or a cloud console. It includes identity providers, cloud management APIs, network and firewall management platforms, virtualization infrastructure, code repositories, CI/CD systems, privileged access management platforms, backup infrastructure, certificate authorities, SaaS administration consoles, and application administration interfaces.

Why It Is Important

Internet-accessible management interfaces can quickly become part of an attack path after credentials are obtained. For example, Azure App Service includes an administrative interface through Kudu Site Control Manager, or SCM, which supports application deployment and management functionality. If an attacker obtains publishing credentials or another identity capable of accessing that interface, automation can quickly test authentication, enumerate functionality, interact with application files, execute commands, retrieve output, and remove staged artifacts.

Similar exposure exists across firewall administration, virtualization consoles, cloud management APIs, backup platforms, CI/CD interfaces, and other management services. Any reachable administrative path gives an automated attacker another capability to test.

Mitigations

Reduce Administrative Internet Exposure: Restrict cloud administration, network device management, application publishing interfaces, hypervisors, backup platforms, and other sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths wherever possible.

Require Trusted Administrative Paths: Require privileged users to administer sensitive infrastructure from managed devices, privileged access workstations, or approved jump hosts. Pair these controls with phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2 or passkeys where supported.

Written by: Tyler McLellan

Introduction

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant investigated a software supply chain compromise campaign targeting the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Technology between April 2026 and July 2026. The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers. Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. This is the first time that we have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with these very short windows, effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning.

The campaign delivered a multi-stage payload chain involving the newly tracked CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor. The threat actor iteratively modified its tradecraft, pivoting its staging infrastructure from cloud providers to dedicated domains and legitimate cloud storage. This evolving staging setup makes it particularly challenging for defenders to establish effective infrastructure-based blocking or network controls. We attribute this activity to a threat cluster we are tracking as UNC7017.

Based on available telemetry, impacted organizations spanned diverse sectors, including IT services, telecommunications, higher education and related entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States. That said, because the campaign attempted to deliver malware to any system polling the update distribution servers during the threat actor’s tampering windows, victimology was opportunistic and likely extends more broadly than the organizations we directly identified.

This campaign was initially identified through collaborative research with the ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), part of Zoho Corporation, whose endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry first detected the activity in late May across multiple customer environments. We thank the METAL team for their proactive telemetry sharing and ongoing collaboration to help secure our mutual customer bases and the broader software ecosystem. Following this joint effort, GTIG notified potentially affected organizations and shared technical findings with AOMEI Technology. AOMEI reported that they took corrective action to secure their distribution servers. METAL’s analysis of this campaign is available in their blog.

How AOMEI Update and Notification Systems Work

AOMEI Backupper provides data backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery, while AnyViewer facilitates remote desktop access and support. Users of these products rely on the ABMarket update flow and its associated background services (Backupper.exe and ABNotify.exe) that periodically poll remote endpoints over HTTPS for update notifications and promotional pop ups:

Figure 1: AOMEI Update Mechanism

Update Configuration (down_html.ini): The software periodically sends an HTTPS request to https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini. This file contains the version number, the MD5 hash of the expected update package, and the URL where the client should download upgrade-now.zip.

Notification Configuration (Notifycfg.ini): The software contacts https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini. This file instructs the local notification process (ABNotify.exe) what messages to display and specifies commands or programs located in the software’s local directory to execute.

Under normal conditions, these files direct the client to download official files hosted on AOMEI’s own domain (www2.aomeisoftware.com).

Campaign Overview

Rather than maintaining a persistent, static modification on the vendor’s distribution servers, GTIG and METAL’s telemetry indicates UNC7017 conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering. We confirmed several tampering windows in 2026, alongside related malware samples observed in the wild starting in late April. However, given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility. Systems checking for updates during an active window received malicious instructions, while systems checking before or after received clean, authentic files.

During the brief tampering windows, the threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates. The threat actor also altered the notification settings file on the update server to abuse the software’s automatic notification service, forcing the system to immediately execute the downloaded malware locally. If a user’s application checked for updates while the threat actor’s modifications were active, then the application would download the trojanized update and execute malware.

In cases where altered configuration files were active, the threat actor directed clients to download a weaponized ZIP archive containing CROSSROAD, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging secondary components. CROSSROAD subsequently established scheduled task persistence to deploy SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor framework delivered via trojanized administration utilities to facilitate covert command and control.

Short Burst Supply Chain Tampering

A defining characteristic of UNC7017's operational security is its reliance on ephemeral, time-compressed server modifications. Across all directly observed waves, the adversary avoided leaving malicious configurations resident on AOMEI's update servers:

May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC)

July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC)

July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC)

At the conclusion of each window, UNC7017 reverted both down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini to their legitimate contents. This hinders post-incident vendor audits, minimizes the window for network defenders to capture live malicious server responses, and restricts compromise to clients polling for updates during those exact minutes.

Weaponizing Native Update Logic: down_html.ini and Configuration Bloat

To compromise endpoints without relying on software vulnerabilities, UNC7017 abused the AOMEI client's legitimate update and popup rendering workflow. By default, the client downloads update archives into its Tmphtml directory, unpacks them to the local html/ directory, and processes instructions from two remote configuration files: down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini.

To ensure the AOMEI client accepted and extracted the weaponized upgrade-now.zip archive, UNC7017 systematically incremented the minor build version (“thrid”) and updated the expected MD5 checksum in down_html.ini during each tampering window:

Malware Delivery & Post-Exploitation Tooling

Across the campaign waves, UNC7017 deployed a consistent chain of custom loaders and commercial/open-source post-exploitation frameworks:

Defense Evasion via Timestomping: Analysis of an early CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) submitted to VirusTotal on May 20 revealed that the threat actor manipulated PE compilation timestamps to display fabricated 2024 build dates in an effort to complicate forensic timeline analysis.

Modified Radmin Server Backdoor: During the May 28 wave, the unsigned loader dropped into the html/ directory executed rsetup64.exe /intsetup, silently installing a modified version of the commercial remote administration tool Radmin Server to establish persistent remote access.

Adaptix C2 Integration: Since at least early July 2026, the threat actor was observed deploying the Adaptix C2 framework across its storage-data.com infrastructure.

The Primary Downloader: CROSSROAD

The primary Stage-2 downloader (upgrade-now.exe, SHA256: 9a58e8f49edf5644e5728f74cf36f560d3d486fa51db4db69d927963c7aca450) is a 64-bit Windows executable written in C, tracked by GTIG as the CROSSROAD malware family. Delivered inside upgrade-now.zip, CROSSROAD is responsible for environment validation, active endpoint cleanup, staging the secondary payload bundle, and establishing scheduled task persistence for the Stage-3 backdoor suite.

Path Verification: As part of its configuration routine, CROSSROAD checks whether its file path contains the substring AOMEI. If the substring is absent, it initiates a self-deletion routine; however, it does not abort, continuing both its background configuration cleanup and its downloader routines regardless.

Execution Guardrails: Before proceeding with secondary downloads, CROSSROAD enforces two primary checks:

Geolocation Check: Queries external domain name system (DNS) (myip.opendns.com, o-o.myaddr.l.google.com) and HTTP reflection services (checkip.amazonaws.com, api.ipify.org, ifconfig.me/ip, icanhazip.com) using custom User-Agents (Anyviewer-loader/1.0, Anyviewer-ipcheck/1.0). In specific execution branches, if the returned country code is "CN" (China), the loader aborts its primary payload execution path.

Lock Mutex: Acquires the named mutex Global\{F9E6E3C0-E11A-4F85-9944-AF4AD6E05883} to prevent multiple concurrent instances on the same host.

Host Artifact Reversion & Anti-Forensics: To complicate post-incident triage and forensic reconstruction, the loader systematically reverts local configuration states during its execution cycle. The malware parses down_html.ini (located at <install_dir>\..\..\), restoring the update thread parameter (thrid) to its default value of 5 and pointing the update download URL back to legitimate AOMEI distribution infrastructure (https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/).

Stage-3 Payload Staging & Extraction: If environment checks pass, CROSSROAD downloads https://promotion.storage-data.com/config/component.zip (also observed as en.zip), to %TEMP%\svc<random_hex>.tmp, and unpacks its contents into the user’s local application data directory using an embedded miniz library.

Persistence via Scheduled Task: To ensure continuous execution of the staged payload bundle, upgrade-now.exe registers a persistent scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime (configured with the description”Radmin Component runtime checkable.”). The task is set to execute %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk every three hours.

Self-Deletion (--nitrod): After extracting the payload bundle and creating the scheduled task, CROSSROAD purges itself from disk. To bypass Windows file-locking constraints, the executable drops a copy of itself to the temporary directory and executes it with the --nitrod parameter, passing its parent PID via NITRODP and original executable path via NITRODT. The child process waits for the parent to terminate, renames the original binary's primary :$DATA stream to an alternate data stream named :wtfbbq via SetFileInformationByHandle, and flags FileDispositionInfo with DeleteFile = TRUE to unlink the binary on handle close.

Version Information: The executable contained standard PE version metadata with a notable typo string: "ProductName: AOMEI Update Compent".

Stage-3 Payload: SHINYROAD and Radmin Suite

The payload archive unpacked into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ by CROSSROAD contains a Famatech Radmin 3.x administration bundle used to deliver the SHINYROAD modular backdoor framework. The malware contains no native persistence mechanism of its own and relies entirely on the external scheduled task registered by CROSSROAD for execution.

Execution via DLL Search-Order Hijacking (BlkScrDl.dll): Execution begins when the persistent RadminComponentRuntime scheduled task launches the legitimate, signed Radmin binary %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk (or FamItrf2.exe). During startup, the Radmin executable is hijacked into loading the attacker's unsigned DLL, BlkScrDl.dll, via search-order hijacking. The adversary named this DLL to masquerade as Radmin's legitimate "blank screen" driver library.

Shared Memory & In-Process COM Server Staging: Upon execution, BlkScrDl.dll locates config.zip in its execution directory, maps its raw contents into a shared memory section named Local\963d3c60-d406-4ad6-aa1e-dc8e45061ccf, and dynamically registers csvc\RuntimeComponent.dll as an in-process COM Server under CLSID {21191641-0D7F-4CD9-9572-01AAE6E7851B} and AppID {9AD3E98A-4C7E-4F37-982D-D73D41E4F91B}.

COM-Triggered Stage-2 Initialization & Embedded PocketPy VM: When the Radmin process instantiates the registered CLSID, the Windows COM subsystem loads the DLL. The DLL reads config.zip directly from shared memory, extracts the encrypted payload metadata.dat, and decrypts it using ChaCha20 with an HMAC-SHA256 derived key and IV. The decrypted payload consists of compiled Python bytecode, which RuntimeComponent.dll executes within an embedded PocketPy interpreter, establishing initial C2 connectivity to 8.218.65.184:443.

Evolution of the SHINYROAD Architecture

Analysis of earlier campaign variants revealed that SHINYROAD relies on custom C-level extensions (_pyio_compat, _pyio_struct, and pkpy) to avoid loading standard Python libraries on disk:

Custom Binary C2 Protocol: Earlier variants communicated over raw TCP (8.218.65.184:41397). The agent generates a unique ID by fingerprinting the hostname and username, authenticates via a hard-coded handshake key, and dynamically transitions all subsequent communication to use symmetric encryption derived from this unique ID.

In-Memory Capabilities: The engine supports interactive remote shell access (os.system), traffic chaffing (generating randomized junk packets to disrupt network signatures), and dynamic in-memory extension via the pkpy WorkPool thread manager without writing script modules to disk.

Outlook and Implications

This campaign highlights a broader evolution in software supply chain attack methodologies. Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines (e.g., SolarWinds, 3CX). While highly impactful, compromised source trees leave persistent binary signatures in official release files that can be discovered during post-release binary analysis.

UNC7017's use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative:

Anti-Analysis by Design: By restricting configuration changes to five to ten minute windows, the vast majority of legitimate users and automated repository crawlers only encounter authentic, vendor-signed files.

Selective Exploitation: Threat actors can selectively compromise target organizations that maintain frequent polling intervals while minimizing their exposure window on vendor infrastructure.

Dual-Pronged Approach: Combining software update redirection with invisible WebDAV NTLM coercion could allow adversaries to harvest credentials from passive users even if binary payload execution is blocked.

Co-opting Commercial Software: Deploying unmodified versions of legitimate administration tools (such as Radmin 3.x) to masquerade sideloaded covert channels illustrates how adversaries blend commercial remote management capabilities with hidden backdoor modules.

Remediation and Hardening

Defenders should focus on behavioral profiling of updater processes, specifically monitoring for unsigned child processes spawned by background update runners and unauthorized network redirection originating from trusted desktop software. For broader recommendations on securing software delivery pipelines, please refer to our previously published Mitigation Guidance for Supply Chain Compromise.

Vendor Notification & Architecture Hardening

On July 17, 2026, Mandiant notified AOMEI Technology regarding the observed configuration tampering on their update infrastructure and provided relevant indicators. AOMEI subsequently responded on July 29, 2026, stating that corrective actions had been taken.

Why Server-Side Remediation Does Not Disinfect Endpoints

Crucially, server-side remediation does not clean endpoints that downloaded malicious updates during earlier tampering windows. Because the tampering occurred in brief, short bursts, systems that received these files may remain compromised without the organization's knowledge unless proactive endpoint hunting and remediation are performed.

Persistent Resident Payloads: Endpoints that polled for updates during an active tampering window downloaded and staged persistent payloads (via scheduled tasks) that remain fully operational even after the vendor restores authentic .ini files on the origin servers.

Obscured Root Cause: While the subsequent backdoor activity and scheduled tasks generate detectable endpoint telemetry, the ephemeral delivery vector obscures the initial intrusion mechanism. Because server tampering lasted approximately 5 minutes—and the loader actively reverted local configuration files—investigators reviewing vendor update URLs hours later will observe only benign, authentic infrastructure, complicating root cause analysis and patient-zero identification.

Hunting Imperative: Organizations running AOMEI software cannot assume they are protected solely because the vendor took corrective server-side action. Enterprise security teams must perform retrospective endpoint and network hunts across the entire April–July time frame using the indicators and YARA rules provided in this post.

Guidance for Software Vendors & Developers

Software supply chain security extends beyond developer workstations and build pipelines. When desktop software relies on remote configuration files to manage update and notification behaviors, adversaries can target the distribution layer rather than the source code. To defend against configuration tampering and distribution-channel hijacking, software vendors should implement the following security controls:

End-to-End Cryptographic Signature Verification: Client applications must cryptographically verify Authenticode digital signatures and validate vendor certificates on all downloaded executables and archives before extraction or execution. Update clients should never rely solely on transport-layer HTTPS or remote checksums (such as cleartext MD5 values in an unauthenticated configuration file).

Cryptographically Signed Configuration Files: Remote configuration files (.ini, .json, or .xml) should be digitally signed using asymmetric public key cryptography. If an origin server or content delivery network (CDN) is modified without authorization, client software will detect the invalid signature and reject the configuration.

Domain Allowlisting and Destination Pinning: Software update clients should enforce strict destination pinning, restricting update downloads exclusively to official, pre-approved vendor domains and CDNs. Update engines should reject redirection to arbitrary third-party domains or generic public cloud storage buckets.

Restricting Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes in In-App Handlers: Embedded web views, promotional popups, and notification handlers should strictly enforce secure web protocols (https://) and explicitly disallow local file (file://) and UNC WebDAV schemes to prevent external NTLM credential coercion.

Decoupling Core Updates from Marketing Channels: Separating essential software maintenance routines from dynamic promotional popups and notification banners reduces the attack surface and ensures that advertising channels cannot trigger local code execution.

Origin Integrity Monitoring and Access Controls: Origin web servers and object storage buckets hosting update metadata should enforce strict access controls, multi-factor authentication, and automated real-time file integrity monitoring (FIM) with immediate alerting on configuration changes.

Guidance for Security Operations (SOC) & Incident Responders

Overcoming the "Point-in-Time" Triage Pitfall

The short-burst nature of this attack creates a unique challenge for incident response:

The Triage Trap: When an EDR alert fires for a suspicious process spawned by an updater, SOC analysts frequently attempt to validate the alert by navigating to the vendor's download URL or checking URL reputation. Because the threat actor reverted the remote configuration files within five to ten minutes, the vendor's server returns authentic, clean files most of the time, leading analysts to mistakenly dismiss the detection as a false positive.

Actionable IR Protocol: Defenders must not rely on live web checks. Incident responders must preserve and analyze the endpoint-cached configuration files in %PROGRAMFILES(X86)%\AOMEI\*\Tmphtml\ and review proxy/firewall telemetry corresponding to the precise second the alert was triggered.

Camouflaged Follow-on Activity

The deployment of Adaptix C2 under the guise of Nitro PDF can mislead analysts into treating alerts as isolated, user-initiated software downloads rather than staged lateral movement. Responders must trace updater parentage to identify root-cause supply chain tampering.
